newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon fires volley at Gulf War arms report.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon fires volley at Gulf War arms report.

text.p: The Pentagon on Tuesday fired back at a congressional report accusing the military of exaggerating the success of F-117A stealth fighters and other high-tech U.S. arms in the 1991 Gulf War.
"The report strikes me as the analytical equivalent of a dumb bomb. It is off target and loud," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.

He conceded there was some exaggeration by the military and arms makers about laser-guided bombs and cruise missiles after the war, but said it did not detract from the fact that "smart" weapons played a key role in defeating Iraq.

The report, released by Congress' General Accounting Office on Monday, said the radar-avoiding F-117A and other arms such as Tomahawk cruise missiles were effective, but that accuracy rates did not match claims made.

The radar-avoiding attack jets, laser-guided bombs and cruise missiles were used by U.S. forces against targets in Baghdad and elsewhere in Iraq during the Gulf War. None of the stealth fighters was lost to Iraqi fire.

"The F-117A bomb hit rate ranged between 41 and 60 percent, which is considered to be highly effective, but is still less than the 80 percent hit rate reported after the war," according to the report by Congress' investigative arm.

It also said early claims of 98 per cent effectiveness for computer chip-guided Tomahawks was exaggerated and "the claim by the Defence Department and contractors of one-target, one-bomb capability for laser-guided munitions was not demonstrated in the air campaign."

"Look, in the fog of war, in the enthusiasm of what happened in the performance of those weapons ... I'm sure that there were statements made by contractors and by people in the military that may have overdramatized their effectiveness," said Bacon.
"It doesn't diminish the fact that they are significantly more effective than non-precision guided munitions."
But he also challenged figures in the report, saying that the GAO had sometimes counted bomb missions that were not flown because of bad weather as target "misses."
"The important point here is that we have moved to a new generation of weaponry. Nobody is going to turn the clock back," he said.
An unclassified version of the GAO report was first released by the New York Times last summer.
The Pentagon conceded in a letter released with Monday's report that there were "shortcomings" in smart weapons and in the military's combat strike assessment capabilities.
"The Defence Department is well along in its programme to correct these shortcomings," it added.
